title: Robotics, Drones and Self-Driving Vehicles
summary: Machines that sense, think and move: how robots work, how drones fly and are regulated, how self-driving vehicles see the road, what robots mean for jobs and safety, and how to program a robot with an algorithm.
learn: What a robot is and the sense-think-act cycle
How robots use sensors, actuators and degrees of freedom
How drones fly, what they're used for and the UK rules for flying them
How self-driving vehicles work and the levels of automation
The impact of robots on jobs, safety and society
How to write and test an algorithm to control a robot
intro: Robots now pack your online shopping, help surgeons operate, spray crops and deliver parcels, while drones film sports and search for missing walkers, and robotaxis carry passengers with no one at the wheel. In this topic you'll find out how robots sense and move, how drones fly and the rules for flying one, how self-driving cars "see", what all this means for jobs and safety, and you'll program a robot yourself.

pages.title: What is a robot?
pages.spec: Define a robot, describe the sense-think-act cycle and give examples of different types of robot
pages.summary: A robot is a programmable machine that can sense its surroundings, make decisions and act in the physical world. Robots range from factory arms to warehouse robots, surgical robots, cobots that work beside people, and humanoid robots.
pages.starter: Is a washing machine a robot? Is a calculator? Is a self-driving car? Discuss what makes something a robot.
sc: I can define what a robot is
I can describe the sense-think-act cycle
I can give examples of different types of robot and where they are used

b: A programmable machine
Senses its surroundings with sensors
Makes decisions with a computer (a controller)
Acts in the physical world with motors and other actuators
Sense: cameras, distance sensors, touch sensors, microphones
Think: a program decides what to do next
Act: wheels turn, arms move, grippers close
Then sense again: the cycle repeats many times a second
Industrial arms: welding and painting cars
Warehouse robots: moving shelves and packing orders
Surgical robots: helping surgeons make tiny, precise movements
Cobots work safely beside people; humanoid robots are being trialled in factories

blocks.text: What is a robot?

A **[[robot]]** is a programmable machine that can sense its environment, make decisions and carry out physical actions, often without a person controlling every step. Robots carry out **[[automation]]**: doing tasks automatically that people once did by hand.
Sense, think, act
Almost every robot follows the **[[sense-think-act]]** cycle:

items: **Sense**: sensors collect information (a camera sees an object, a bumper detects a wall).
**Think**: the controller (a small computer) runs a program to decide what to do.
**Act**: actuators such as motors move wheels, arms or grippers.

blocks.text: The cycle repeats many times every second, so the robot can react to changes.
Types of robot

blocks.caption: Robots in the real world
head: Type
What it does
Example
rows: Welding car bodies in a factory
Robots in online-shopping warehouses picking and moving orders
Lets a surgeon make tiny, steady movements
Works safely beside people, slowing or stopping if touched
Helping workers lift and assemble parts
Robot vacuum cleaners, lawnmowers, hospital delivery robots
Has a human-like body to work in spaces built for people
Humanoid robots being trialled in car factories and warehouses

blocks.text: Is a washing machine a robot? It follows a program and uses sensors, but it can't move around or change what it does much. Most people call it an automated machine rather than a robot. The line isn't always sharp!

blocks.title: Robot or not?
steps: Sort the 10 picture cards (e.g. robot vacuum, toaster, drone, factory arm, remote-control car, smart speaker) into "robot", "not a robot" and "not sure".
For each robot, identify what it senses, how it thinks and how it acts.
Agree a one-sentence class definition of a robot.

q.q: Explain why a robot vacuum is a robot but a toaster isn't.
q.a: The vacuum senses obstacles and dirt, decides where to go with a program and moves itself (sense-think-act); the toaster just follows a timer and doesn't sense its surroundings or move.

q.q: Is a remote-control car a robot? Explain.
q.a: Not really: a person makes all the decisions. If it had sensors and a program to drive itself, it would be a robot.

check.q: What is a robot?
o: A programmable machine that senses, decides and acts

check.q: What are the three steps of the robot cycle?
What is a cobot?
o: A robot designed to work safely beside people

check.q: Which is an example of a surgical robot's advantage?

practice.a: A programmable machine (1) that senses its environment, makes decisions and acts physically (1).

practice.q: Describe the sense-think-act cycle for a robot vacuum cleaner.
practice.a: Sense: bump/distance/dirt sensors detect obstacles and dirt (1); think: program decides to turn or clean more (1); act: motors turn wheels/brushes (1).

pages.title: How robots sense and move
pages.spec: Describe the sensors robots use, how they move, and the meaning of degrees of freedom and accuracy
pages.summary: Robots use sensors such as cameras, lidar, ultrasonic sensors, touch sensors and encoders to understand their surroundings and their own position. Motors and grippers let them move; the number of ways a robot can move is called its degrees of freedom.
pages.starter: Close your eyes and touch your nose. How did you know where your hand was?
sc: I can name sensors robots use and what each is for
I can explain degrees of freedom
I can explain why precision and repeatability matter

b: Cameras plus computer vision: recognise objects and people
Lidar: laser pulses measure distances to build a 3D map
Ultrasonic and infrared: measure distance to nearby objects
Touch and force sensors: feel contact and grip strength
Encoders count how far each wheel or joint has turned
IMUs (accelerometers and gyroscopes) sense tilt and movement
GPS for outdoor robots; maps for indoor ones
Combining sensors gives a more reliable picture
Motors turn wheels, joints and propellers
Degrees of freedom: the number of independent ways a robot can move
A typical factory arm has 6 degrees of freedom
The end effector is the "hand": a gripper, welder, suction cup or tool

blocks.text: Robot sensors

blocks.caption: How robots sense the world
head: Sensor
How it works
Used for
rows: Recognising objects, reading labels, spotting people
Fires laser pulses and times their reflections
Times how long a sound pulse takes to echo back
Counts how far a wheel or joint has turned
Accelerometer and gyroscope sense movement and tilt

blocks.text: Robots often combine several sensors (called sensor fusion), so if one is fooled (a camera in the dark, say) others can fill the gap.
Movement

A robot's **[[degrees of freedom]]** are the number of independent ways it can move. Your arm has about 7 (shoulder, elbow, wrist). Most factory robot arms have 6, which lets them reach a point from almost any angle. The tool on the end of a robot arm is the **[[end effector]]**: it might be a gripper, a suction cup, a paint sprayer or a welding torch.
Precision and repeatability

Industrial robots are valued because they're precise (they go exactly where they're told) and repeatable (they do it the same way thousands of times). Surgical robots also scale down a surgeon's hand movements and filter out any tremor.

blocks.title: Working out distance with an ultrasonic sensor
blocks.context: Sound travels at about 340 metres per second. An echo comes back after 0.01 seconds.
steps: Total distance travelled by the sound = 340 × 0.01 = 3.4 m.
The sound went there and back, so divide by 2.

blocks.title: Sensor match-up
steps: Read the six robot missions (e.g. a robot that picks ripe strawberries, a robot that cleans a swimming pool, a delivery robot crossing a pavement).
Choose the sensors each robot needs and explain why.
Choose an end effector for each robot that has an arm.
Identify one situation where a sensor could be fooled, and which other sensor would help.

q.q: Which sensors does a strawberry-picking robot need, and why?
q.a: A camera with computer vision to find ripe (red) strawberries; a force sensor in the gripper so it doesn't squash them; encoders so the arm knows its position.

q.q: Describe a situation where a sensor could be fooled.
q.a: E.g. a camera on a delivery robot can't see well at night or in fog; lidar or ultrasonic sensors can still measure distances to obstacles.

check.q: What does lidar use to measure distance?
What does an encoder measure?
o: How far a wheel or joint has turned

check.q: What are degrees of freedom?
o: The number of independent ways a robot can move
How free the robot is to leave

check.q: What is an end effector?
o: The tool on the end of a robot arm

practice.q: Explain why a robot might use more than one type of sensor.
practice.a: One sensor can be fooled or fail in some conditions (1); combining sensors gives a more reliable picture (1).

practice.q: An ultrasonic echo returns after 0.02 s. Sound travels at 340 m/s. Calculate the distance to the obstacle.
practice.a: 340 × 0.02 = 6.8 m (1); halve for there and back (1); 3.4 m (1).

pages.title: Drones
pages.spec: Explain how drones fly, describe their uses and apply the UK rules for flying a drone safely
pages.summary: Most drones are quadcopters that steer by changing the speed of four rotors. Drones are used for filming, farming, inspections, deliveries and search and rescue. In the UK, flyers must follow the Drone Code, and most need a Flyer ID and Operator ID from the Civil Aviation Authority.
pages.starter: Name three jobs a drone could do better, faster or more safely than a person.
sc: I can explain how a quadcopter moves
I can describe uses of drones
I can apply the UK Drone Code

b: Four rotors: two spin clockwise, two anticlockwise
All faster: rise; all slower: descend
Tilt by speeding up rotors on one side: the drone moves that way
A flight controller with an IMU makes hundreds of tiny adjustments a second
Search and rescue: thermal cameras find missing people
Farming: crop monitoring and precision spraying
Inspections: wind turbines, bridges, power lines
Deliveries: medicines and blood samples between hospitals; trials of parcel delivery
Get your Flyer ID (free online test) and Operator ID from the CAA
Never fly higher than 120 m (400 ft)
Keep the drone in sight at all times
Stay away from airports, crowds and people; respect privacy

blocks.text: How drones fly

A **[[drone]]** is an aircraft without a pilot on board, controlled remotely or flying itself. Most small drones are **[[quadcopter|quadcopters]]** with four rotors. Two spin clockwise and two anticlockwise, so the drone doesn't spin round.

blocks.caption: Controlling a quadcopter
head: Movement
What the rotors do
rows: Rear rotors speed up, so the drone tilts forward
Clockwise pair and anticlockwise pair change speed relative to each other

blocks.text: A flight controller uses an IMU and GPS to make hundreds of tiny adjustments every second, which is why modern drones can hover almost perfectly still.
What drones are used for

blocks.title: Drone uses
items: Search and rescue: thermal cameras find missing people on mountains or at sea
Farming: checking crop health and spraying only where needed
Inspections: wind turbines, bridges and power lines without climbing
Deliveries: medical supplies between hospitals and to islands; parcel delivery trials
Filming and mapping: sport, films, surveying land
Drone light shows replacing fireworks

blocks.text: The UK Drone Code

The **Civil Aviation Authority (CAA)** sets the rules for drones in the UK. From 2026, anyone flying a drone weighing 100 g or more must pass a free online test to get a **[[Flyer ID]]**, and the person responsible for the drone needs an **[[Operator ID]]** (the owner must be 18 or over). Always check the latest rules on the CAA website before flying.

blocks.title: Key rules of the Drone Code
items: Never fly higher than 120 metres (400 feet)
Always keep the drone in **[[visual line of sight]]**: you must be able to see it
Never fly near airports or airfields
Keep a safe distance from people and never fly over crowds
Respect privacy: don't film people without permission

blocks.text: Flying a drone near an airport can put aircraft and lives in danger, and is a serious criminal offence.

blocks.title: Mission control
steps: Your team is planning a drone mission to find a lost walker on Cuilcagh Mountain.
Choose the drone features you need (camera type, battery, GPS, speaker).
Plan your flight using the Drone Code: height, line of sight, people and permissions.
Identify two risks and how you'd reduce them.

q.q: Which drone features do you need, and why?
q.a: Thermal camera to spot body heat; GPS to map the search and return home; long battery life or spare batteries; a speaker to talk to the walker; lights for poor visibility.

q.q: Describe two risks and how you'd reduce them.
q.a: E.g. losing sight of the drone in cloud: use spotters and stay within line of sight; strong wind draining battery: check the weather and set an automatic return-home battery level.

check.q: How many rotors does a quadcopter have?
What is the maximum height for most drone flights in the UK?
What does visual line of sight mean?
o: You must film in straight lines
You must be able to see the drone at all times

check.q: Which organisation sets UK drone rules?

practice.q: Explain how a quadcopter rises and moves forward.
practice.a: Rise: all four rotors speed up (1); forward: rear rotors speed up, tilting it forward (1).

practice.q: Describe three rules a drone flyer in the UK must follow.
practice.a: Any three: below 120 m (1); keep in visual line of sight (1); away from airports (1); away from people/crowds (1); Flyer ID/Operator ID (1); respect privacy (1).

pages.title: Self-driving vehicles
pages.spec: Describe how self-driving vehicles perceive, plan and act, and explain the levels of driving automation
pages.summary: Self-driving vehicles use cameras, radar, lidar and AI to perceive the road, predict what others will do, plan a path and control the car. Driving automation is described in levels 0 to 5. Robotaxis already carry passengers in some cities, and the UK's Automated Vehicles Act 2024 sets out who is responsible when a car drives itself.
pages.starter: What does a human driver need to notice in the first ten seconds of pulling out of a junction?
sc: I can describe how a self-driving car senses its surroundings
I can explain the levels of driving automation
I can describe the benefits and challenges of self-driving vehicles

b: Cameras: colours, lanes, signs and traffic lights
Radar: distance and speed of other vehicles, even in rain and fog
Lidar: a precise 3D map of everything around the car
AI combines them to perceive, predict, plan and control
Level 0-2: the human drives; the car helps (e.g. lane-keeping, adaptive cruise control)
Level 3: the car drives in some conditions; the human must take over when asked
Level 4: the car drives itself fully in a defined area, e.g. a robotaxi zone
Level 5: drives anywhere, any conditions (not yet achieved)
Robotaxis already carry paying passengers in some US and Chinese cities
UK: the Automated Vehicles Act 2024; pilots of self-driving taxi services
When the car drives itself, the company, not the passenger, is responsible
Challenges: edge cases, bad weather, cost, trust, jobs

blocks.text: How self-driving works
An **[[autonomous vehicle]]** can drive itself without human control. It uses several sensors:

blocks.caption: Self-driving sensors
head: Sensor
Good at
Weakness
rows: Colours, lane lines, signs, traffic lights
Struggles in darkness, glare and fog
Distance and speed of objects, works in rain and fog
Expensive; affected by heavy rain or snow

blocks.text: AI software runs four stages many times a second: **perceive** (what's around me?), **predict** (what will that cyclist do next?), **plan** (what path should I take?) and **control** (steer, brake, accelerate).
Levels of automation

blocks.caption: The levels of driving automation (SAE levels)
head: Level
Who drives?
Example
rows: Human only; the car may give warnings
Human, with help steering OR speed
Human must supervise; car steers AND controls speed
Car drives in set conditions; human must take over when asked
Car drives fully in a defined area; no human needed there
Car drives anywhere, in any conditions

blocks.text: These are often called the **[[levels of automation]]**. Many cars on sale have level 2 features, but the driver is still fully responsible.
Robotaxis and the law

A **[[robotaxi]]** is a driverless taxi. Robotaxi services already carry paying passengers in several US and Chinese cities, and companies plan services in UK cities. The UK's **Automated Vehicles Act 2024** sets out that when a vehicle is legally driving itself, the authorised company is responsible for how it drives, not the person sitting in it.
Benefits and challenges

blocks.title: Weighing up self-driving vehicles
items: Benefit: most crashes involve human error, so automation could save lives
Benefit: independence for people who can't drive (e.g. some disabled or older people)
Challenge: **[[edge case|Edge cases]]**, rare unusual situations like a horse on the road or a police officer waving traffic through
Challenge: rural roads, bad weather and poor road markings
Challenge: trust, cost, cyber security and jobs for drivers

blocks.title: Edge case challenge
steps: Read the eight driving scenarios (e.g. a ball rolling into the road, a tractor on a narrow country lane, roadworks with a person holding a stop sign).
For each, decide what the car must perceive, predict and do.
Rate how hard each would be for a self-driving car (1-5) and explain why.
Decide which would be hardest on Fermanagh's rural roads.

q.q: What should the car predict when a ball rolls into the road?
q.a: That a child may run out after it, so it should slow down and be ready to stop, even if no person is visible yet.

q.q: Which scenario is hardest on rural roads, and why?
q.a: E.g. the tractor on a narrow lane: no lane markings, limited space to pass, and the car must judge whether to reverse to a passing place or wait; poor mobile signal and mapping may also make it harder.

check.q: Which sensor works best in fog and rain?
At which level does the car drive fully, but only in a defined area?
What is an edge case?
o: A rare, unusual situation that's hard to handle

check.q: Under the UK Automated Vehicles Act 2024, who is responsible when the vehicle is driving itself?

practice.q: Describe the four stages a self-driving car's software goes through.
practice.a: Perceive: work out what's around it (1); predict: what others will do (1); plan: choose a path (1); control: steer/brake/accelerate (1).

practice.q: Discuss whether self-driving cars should be allowed on rural roads in Northern Ireland.
practice.a: Benefits, e.g. fewer crashes, independence for non-drivers (1-2); challenges, e.g. narrow lanes, poor markings, weather, signal, edge cases (1-2); conclusion (1). Max 4.

pages.title: Robots and society
pages.spec: Evaluate the impact of robots and automation on jobs, safety and society
pages.summary: Robots can take on dull, dirty and dangerous work and boost productivity, but automation also changes and replaces jobs. Society must decide who is responsible when robots cause harm, how to keep people safe, and whether some decisions should never be left to machines.
pages.starter: Would you rather a robot or a person did these jobs: bin collector, nurse, surgeon, teacher, soldier? Why?
sc: I can describe the impact of robots on jobs
I can discuss safety and responsibility when robots go wrong
I can form a reasoned opinion on an ethical question about robots

b: Robots are ideal for dull, dirty and dangerous work
Dull: repetitive packing and sorting
Dirty: sewer inspection, cleaning tanks
Dangerous: bomb disposal, nuclear clean-up, deep sea, space
Some jobs disappear or shrink (job displacement)
Many jobs change: people work alongside robots
New jobs appear: robot technicians, programmers, designers
The big question: who benefits, and who gets retrained?
If a robot causes harm, who is accountable: maker, programmer, owner or user?
Safety standards, testing and emergency stops
Some decisions may need a "human in the loop"
Should robots ever make life-or-death decisions?

blocks.text: Dull, dirty and dangerous

Robots are especially useful for work that is **[[dull, dirty and dangerous]]**: repetitive tasks, unpleasant environments and situations that put people at risk. Robots have explored the Fukushima nuclear plant after the 2011 disaster, defused bombs, inspected sewers and explored Mars.
Robots and jobs
**[[job displacement|Job displacement]]** happens when people's jobs are replaced by machines. History shows that new technology removes some jobs but also creates new ones and changes many more.

blocks.caption: How automation affects work
head: Effect
Example
rows: Fewer workers needed to pack orders in automated warehouses
Farmers use drones and robotic milking, spending more time on planning and animal care
Robot technicians, programmers, drone pilots, AI safety testers
Creativity, care, problem-solving, communication, digital skills

blocks.text: Safety and responsibility

**[[accountability|Accountability]]** means being responsible for what happens. When a robot or self-driving car causes harm, it can be hard to decide who is to blame: the company that made it, the programmer, the owner or the user. Laws like the UK's Automated Vehicles Act try to make this clear.

blocks.title: Keeping people safe around robots
items: Testing in simulation and in controlled spaces before real use
Emergency stop buttons and safety zones around industrial robots
Cobots designed to slow down or stop when they touch a person
A "human in the loop" for important decisions

blocks.text: Ethical questions

**[[ethics|Ethics]]** is about deciding what is right and wrong. Robots raise big ethical questions. Should robots care for older people? Should armed robots be allowed to choose targets? Who should get the money saved by automation?

blocks.title: Robot debate
steps: Your group is given a motion, e.g. "Care homes should use robots to look after residents" or "Delivery robots should be allowed on all pavements".
Prepare two arguments for and two against, using evidence from this topic.
Hold a short debate with another group.
Write your own conclusion, giving reasons.

q.q: Write your strongest argument for and against your motion.
q.a: E.g. care robots: For: they can lift residents safely and give reminders 24/7, freeing staff for personal care. Against: residents may feel lonely without human contact, and robots can't notice subtle signs of illness or distress.
A balanced judgement, e.g. "Robots should help with lifting and reminders, but they must not replace human carers, because care needs empathy and judgement."

check.q: What are the "three Ds" of robot work?
What is job displacement?
o: People's jobs being replaced by machines

check.q: Which job has been created by robotics?
What does accountability mean?
check.why: Who is to blame if harm occurs?

practice.q: Give two examples of dangerous jobs that robots can do.
practice.a: Any two: bomb disposal (1); nuclear clean-up (1); deep-sea/space exploration (1); sewer/tank inspection (1); firefighting (1).

practice.q: "Robots will take all our jobs." Evaluate this statement.
practice.a: Some jobs replaced/reduced (1); many jobs changed rather than lost (1); new jobs created (1); conclusion: overstated, but retraining/skills matter (1).

pages.title: Program a robot
pages.spec: Design, write and test an algorithm to control a robot using sequence, selection and iteration
pages.summary: Robots follow algorithms. Programmers use sequence, selection (IF) and iteration (loops) with sensor readings to control robots, then test and debug them. A line-following robot is a classic example of selection inside a loop.
pages.starter: Write instructions to guide a blindfolded partner from the door to your desk. What went wrong?
sc: I can write an algorithm to control a robot
I can use sequence, selection and iteration with sensor inputs
I can test and debug a robot program

b: An algorithm is a precise set of steps
Sequence: steps in order (forward 50 cm, turn right 90°)
Selection: IF a sensor detects something THEN do this ELSE do that
Iteration: repeat (a loop) so the robot keeps reacting
Two light sensors look down at a black line
IF left sensor sees black THEN turn left
ELSE IF right sensor sees black THEN turn right
ELSE go forward ... REPEAT forever
Test in a simulation first
Then test on the real robot, one part at a time
Record what you expected vs what happened
Real robots slip, batteries fade, and lighting changes sensor readings

blocks.text: Algorithms for robots
An **[[algorithm]]** is a precise set of steps to solve a problem. Robot programs combine:

items: **Sequence**: instructions in the right order.
**[[selection|Selection]]**: making a decision using IF ... THEN ... ELSE, usually based on a sensor reading.
**[[iteration|Iteration]]**: repeating instructions with a loop, so the robot keeps sensing and reacting.

blocks.title: Obstacle avoider
blocks.context: A robot has a distance sensor on its front and should explore a room without crashing.
steps: REPEAT FOREVER
distance ← read distance sensor
IF distance < 20 cm THEN stop, reverse 10 cm, turn right 90°
ELSE move forward
blocks.answer: The loop (iteration) keeps checking the sensor; the IF (selection) decides whether to avoid or keep going.

blocks.text: Line-following
A line-following robot uses two light or infrared sensors pointing at the floor. A black line reflects less light than a white floor.

items: IF the left sensor sees black THEN turn left.
ELSE IF the right sensor sees black THEN turn right.
ELSE drive forward.
Repeat forever.

blocks.text: Testing and debugging

**[[debugging|Debugging]]** means finding and fixing errors. Robots are tricky to debug because the real world is messy: wheels slip, batteries run down and lighting changes sensor readings. Engineers often test first in a **[[simulation]]**, a computer model of the robot and its world, which is quicker, cheaper and safer.
With BBC micro:bits and a robot buggy kit, or an online robot simulator, you can test these algorithms for real. Change one thing at a time and record what happens.

blocks.title: Code the robot
steps: Choose a challenge: escape a maze, follow a line, or patrol a room avoiding obstacles.
Write your algorithm in pseudocode or a flowchart, using sequence, selection and iteration.
Test it (in a simulator, with a micro:bit buggy, or by "playing robot" with a partner).
Record one bug, how you found it and how you fixed it.

q.a: E.g. maze (left-hand rule): REPEAT UNTIL exit found: IF no wall on left THEN turn left and move forward; ELSE IF no wall ahead THEN move forward; ELSE turn right.

q.q: Describe one bug and how you fixed it.
q.a: E.g. "The robot turned too far because the motors kept going after the turn command. We reduced the turn time and tested again until it turned 90°."

check.q: What does selection mean in a robot program?
o: Making a decision with IF ... THEN ... ELSE

check.q: Why do robot programs usually use a loop?
o: So the robot keeps sensing and reacting

check.q: How does a line-following robot detect a black line?
o: Light sensors detect less reflected light

check.q: Why test a robot in a simulation first?

practice.q: Write an algorithm for a robot that stops when an object is less than 10 cm away and otherwise moves forward.
practice.a: Loop/repeat (1); read distance sensor and IF distance < 10 THEN stop (1); ELSE move forward (1).

practice.q: Explain why a robot that works in a simulation might fail in real life.
practice.a: Real world differences, e.g. wheels slip, battery fades, lighting/sensor noise (1); the simulation doesn't model everything perfectly (1).
